articles.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon told friend if he killed anyone he’d dump belongings in bin and take bodies to bushland, court hears
articles.summary: Former police officer has pleaded not guilty to murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies in early 2024 – nine months after discussion with friend Georgia Cook

blocks.text: A Sydney police officer told a friend he would hide the bodies of anyone he killed in bushland and put their belongings in a dumpster, months before allegedly murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies, a court has been told.
Beau Lamarre-Condon, 31, has been accused of fatally shooting the couple with a police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024.
He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.
At his double murder trial on Monday, Georgia Cook, a close friend of Lamarre-Condon, told the NSW supreme court about a dinner in May 2023.
The brief relationship between Baird and Lamarre-Condon had ended when the accused asked her what she would do if he told her he’d killed someone, Cook told the jury.
He then asked what she would do if she killed someone and what she would do with their bodies, the court heard. Cook responded she had no idea.

She said on Monday that Lamarre-Condon replied: “After I’d killed them I would take their stuff, I would put it in a dumpster, and I would take their bodies in bushland where nobody would ever find them.”
Asked about her response, Cook said the situation in 2023 felt “very surreal”.
“I didn’t know whether to believe anything I’d heard, or whether it was true,” she told the jury.
“Hearing a person of power in the police force [say that] – it felt like I didn’t have anywhere to go and I was really scared by what I had heard.”
after newsletter promotion

After Lamarre-Condon allegedly shot Baird and Davies in February 2024, he dumped Baird’s bloodied belongings and furniture into a skip bin in Cronulla, the prosecution said during its opening statement last week.
The two bodies were found on the fence line of a Greek orthodox monastery in remote bushland in Bungonia – about 200km from Paddington.

Cook on Friday told the court that Lamarre-Condon told her he had been watching Baird from outside his home. The crown alleged in its opening that the police officeer began planning to murder Baird in early 2024.
The defence team has claimed he was acting in self-defence after he disguised himself as an UberEats rider and entered Baird’s home on the day of the shootings.
The trial before justice Natalie Adams continues.

articles.title: Rains forecast over Visayas, parts of Mindanao as ITCZ prevails
articles.summary: The ITCZ is forecast to bring scattered rains and thunderstorms to the Visayas, Palawan and parts of Mindanao on Monday.

blocks.text: September 28, 2026 | 8:59am
Satellite-based rendering shows the relative location of cyclone Surigae (formerly 'Queenie) north of the Philippines as of 8:50 a.m. on Monday, Sept. 28, 2026.
JMA

MANILA, Philippines — The intertropical convergence zone is forecast to bring scattered rains and thunderstorms over the Visayas, Palawan and parts of Mindanao on Monday, September 28, with possible flash floods or landslides during moderate to at times heavy rains.
In its 4 a.m. weather forecast, PAGASA said the ITCZ is affecting Palawan, the Visayas and Mindanao.
The ICTZ is a weather system of converging winds that force air upward, creating heavy clouds, thunderstorms and rainfall.
Cloudy skies with scattered rains and thunderstorms are forecast over the Visayas, Zamboanga Peninsula, Northern Mindanao, Caraga, Palawan and Lanao del Sur.
PAGASA warned that moderate to at times heavy rains in these areas could trigger flash floods or landslides.
The rest of Mindanao is forecast to have partly cloudy to cloudy skies with isolated rain showers or thunderstorms due to the ITCZ. Flash floods or landslides may occur during severe thunderstorms.
Metro Manila and the rest of Luzon, meanwhile, may experience partly cloudy to cloudy skies with isolated rain showers or thunderstorms caused by localized thunderstorms.
PAGASA also warned of possible flash floods or landslides during severe thunderstorms in these areas.
Typhoon remains outside PAR
Typhoon Surigae, formerly known as Queenie while inside the Philippine area of responsibility, remained outside PAR early Monday.
As of 3 a.m., the typhoon was located 1,055 kilometers northeast of extreme northern Luzon.
Surigae was packing maximum sustained winds of 175 kilometers per hour near the center, with gusts of up to 215 kph. It was moving east-northeastward at 15 kph.
PAGASA said winds across Luzon will be light to moderate and variable, with slight to moderate coastal waters ranging from 0.6 to 1.5 meters.
The Visayas and Mindanao will likewise have light to moderate winds, blowing from the southeast to southwest, with coastal waters of 0.6 to 1.5 meters.

articles.title: Trump asked Xi Jinping if China would like to buy US weapons, American ambassador says
articles.summary:
David Perdue’s remarks come after a Taiwanese minister spoke of the ‘severe’ military threat posed by Beijing to the self-ruled island

Donald Trump offered to sell weapons to China while…

blocks.text: Donald Trump offered to sell weapons to China while hosting its leader, Xi Jinping, last week, the US ambassador to China said on Sunday.
David Perdue told Fox News on Sunday: “President Trump continues to say, hey, we sell arms to other people around the world. He actually asked President Xi, would he like to buy some at one point.”

The extraordinary claim came during an interview about US policy on Taiwan, which has been waiting for months for Trump to approve a new arms sales ⁠package worth $14bn, after a record multi-billion dollar deal was unveiled in December last year.

Trump’s level of commitment to protecting Taiwan has previously been questioned. At a meeting with Xi in Beijing in May, ⁠Trump said he was keeping the $14bn Taiwan arms sales package in abeyance, describing it as a “very good negotiating chip” in dealings with China.

Washington has long maintained a strategically ambiguous stance on whether it would defend Taiwan in the event of an invasion. But under the decades-old Taiwan Relations Act, it is required to provide Taipei with sufficient military equipment to defend itself.

Beijing has repeatedly said it “resolutely opposes” Washington’s arms sales to the island democracy, which it regards as a breakaway province, despite never having ruled it, and has not renounced the use of force to take. During their Washington meeting last week, Xi urged Trump to oppose “Taiwan independence,” according to a readout from the official Chinese news agency Xinhua.

After Purdue’s interview, the White House told the New York Times that the US had no plans to sell arms to China, while the state department said: “US law prohibits arms sales to China and there is no offer or plan to sell arms to China.”
Before the interview, Taiwanese deputy foreign minister Chen Ming-chi spoke of the severe military threat China posed.

“Taiwan faces a severe situation in the Taiwan strait. Even though China’s economy is declining, it continues investing more resources into building military capacity. Under ‌this context, the US very much understands our defence needs,” he told reporters in Taipei.
Trump ​has not mentioned the sale ‌since last week’s summit, saying ‌only on Saturday that Xi understands his position on Taiwan.
Perdue himself told CNBC ​on Friday that there had been ​no change in Taiwan policy by Trump, including on arms ​sales.
With Reuters

articles.title: Protesters disperse after blocking route for loyalist march in Portadown
articles.summary:
Talks expected on Monday after Sinn Féin leaders join those on streets opposing decision to allow Orange Order parade for first time since 1998

Hundreds of protesters spent the day blocking…
articles.byline: Mark Brown, Lisa O’Carroll and Shane Harrison

blocks.text: Hundreds of protesters spent the day blocking the route of a hugely contentious parade in Northern Ireland after a court gave late-night clearance for the Orange Order to march on a historically significant road for the first time in nearly 30 years.

The loyalist Drumcree parade along the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road in Portadown was given the go-ahead by the Parades Commission for the first time since 1998, a decision denounced by Sinn Féin as “madness”.
It led to a weekend of intense legal wrangling which concluded at 2.15am on Sunday when the court of appeal said it could not interfere with the commission’s decision.

In driving rain on a cold Sunday morning, hundreds of nationalist protesters gathered to block the route. Many linked arms and sang songs as announcements were made over loudspeaker that they were liable to arrest and prosecution.
The Orangemen spent the day ensconced a mile away in a church, the proposed start of the march, and said they would wait until police told them the road was clear.

The standoff lasted throughout Sunday, with protesters largely dispersing in the early hours of Monday, when Breandán Mac Cionnaith, from the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition, said he had received “commitments” that the parade would not be proceeding down the road overnight.
Mac Cionnaith told protesters he would meet the Northern Ireland secretary, Chris Bryant, and Police Service of Northern Ireland chief constable Jon Boutcher on Monday morning for talks.
Michelle O’Neill, the Sinn Féin vice-president and Northern Ireland first minister, told reporters shortly after midnight that the Garvaghy Road community had won a “victory”.

blocks.caption: Portadown Orangemen at Drumcree Church start their march towards Garvaghy Road, which was stopped a short distance later by police. Photograph: Paul Faith/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Among the protesters earlier in the day was the Sinn Féin president, Mary Lou McDonald, who said the decision to allow the parade was “madness” and “primitive treatment of any community in the year 2026. It is intolerable, and it will not be tolerated.”

She added: “The mood here has been peaceful. It has been united and orderly. This is a dignified and united community and they are absolutely determined that they and we will not be drawn back into the past.”

blocks.caption: Michelle O’Neill (centre) and Mary Lou McDonald (right) speak to the media in Portadown. Photograph: Charles McQuillan/Getty Images

blocks.text: O’Neill was also there and said reigniting the dispute brought “into question how this whole peace process works”. She told reporters: “We’re meeting families who feel collectively traumatised, who feel individually traumatised. Does anybody think that this is a good idea?

“No right-minded person would make this decision. I still do not know the answer to this question – why, after 28 years of a determination to block a march down this road, the Parades Commission thought that this was the right idea today to bring this mess back on to this community.”
The local Democratic Unionist party (DUP) MP, Carla Lockhart, accused O’Neill of “whipping up hysteria” at an “unlawful” protest.
“It is unreal that we have a first minister behaving the way she is behaving,” she said. “If I did it, or if any of my colleagues did it, I would be in the back of a Land Rover.”

blocks.caption: Nationalist protesters gathered in Portadown. Photograph: Charles McQuillan/Getty Images

blocks.text: Gavin Robinson, the DUP leader, said: “We now have lawmakers acting as law breakers,” and he accused O’Neill of “giving two fingers to the courts, the police, the rule of law”.

Bryant cut short his attendance at the Labour party conference in Liverpool to travel to Belfast, but said he did not have the powers to call the march off unless police formally requested him to do so. He said the nationalist protest was unlawful and called on politicians to “calm things down”.

Bryant said: “It is incumbent on everybody in political office to take this moment very, very seriously and to take the temperature down, to think twice before … inflating any argument and to think about what somebody else who doesn’t share your opinion might think about the way you’ve put your case.”

blocks.caption: Protesters hold banners on Garvaghy Road. Photograph: Charles McQuillan/Getty Images

blocks.text: Earlier in the day the tense standoff drew in the prime minister, Andy Burnham, who appealed for “calm on all sides”.
The Irish taoiseach, Mícheál Martin, echoed that but described the Parades Commission decision as “incomprehensible and wrong”.
He called for the situation to be mediated sensibly in a way “that protects the gains that have been made and the peace and harmony that has prevailed for so long”.
The Drumcree parade on the Garvaghy Road – a Catholic enclave in a largely Protestant town – sparked some of the most serious and violent disorder in Northern Ireland’s history.
On Friday, the Parades Commission granted permission subject to restrictions, including a limit of 35 participants, an 8am start time instead of 1pm, and that it should be held in silence.

blocks.caption: Nigel Dawson, known as the district master of Portadown Loyal Orange Lodge, speaks to a police officer. Photograph: Cathal McNaughton/Reuters

blocks.text: The decision was challenged and blocked on Saturday by a judge, Justice Patricia Smyth, who said the “long-running dispute has the potential to escalate” across Northern Ireland.
That decision was then challenged by the Orange Order, leading to two further hearings on Saturday night and Sunday morning.

The final, time-limited sitting, which began at 20 minutes past midnight on Sunday, was heard before Mr Justice Humphreys, who acknowledged the “unusual if not unprecedented circumstances … with a parade scheduled to begin in just over six hours’ time”.
Outlining his decision, Humphreys cited case law that as a public body the courts must respect the commission’s judgment and “their decisions will not be lightly interfered with”.

articles.title: Northeast U.S. pummelled by wind and floods from deadly nor'easter
articles.summary: Residents of coastal communities in the U.S. northeast slogged through floodwaters for a second day as a powerful nor'easter pummelled the shoreline Sunday, knocking out power to tens of thousands of…

image.caption: A pedestrian and a car navigate a street as a wave crashes into a seawall in Hampton, N.H., on Sunday. (C.J. Gunther/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

Residents of coastal communities in the U.S. northeast slogged through floodwaters for a second day as a powerful nor'easter pummelled the shoreline Sunday, knocking out power to tens of thousands of homes.
New York City housing authority worker died after falling from tree
Tidal surges swamped low-lying neighbourhoods in New Jersey while wind gusts toppled trees on New York's Long Island, damaging homes and bringing down utility poles.

In the New Jersey beach town of Sea Bright, each high tide brought a new round of flooding. "It's not like a one-time occurrence," said Caroline Virenius, whose garage filled with about a foot of water. "It's getting wet again and again."

The slow-moving storm, which killed a New York City housing authority worker when a tree fell Saturday, was expected to linger through Sunday with heavy rain, strong winds and dangerous surf all the way to New England.

Extreme amounts of rain — more than 10 centimetres since Friday in some spots in New Jersey — combined with a surging ocean led to flooding amounts not seen for close to a decade in places used to dealing with high water, residents said.
Flights, utilities affected

The nor'easter triggered memories of Superstorm Sandy, which left behind over $60 billion US in damage across the eastern U.S. in 2012. While this storm's impact has been nowhere near that, it could be the first of several along the East Coast this fall because of an El Niño climate pattern that's disrupting this year's weather.
Images of waves crashing into sea walls and onto beaches raised concerns about coastal erosion.

items: Powerful storm causes widespread flooding, outages in northeast U.S.

blocks.text: Well over 100,000 customers were without power across the Northeast and mid-Atlantic at times on Sunday, according to PowerOutage.us. The most widespread outages were in counties along the coast from New Jersey to Connecticut.

Numerous flights were cancelled or delayed up and down the coast. More than 250 flights had been cancelled at Boston Logan International Airport by late Sunday morning as wind gusts reached 64 km/h, according to the Massachusetts Port Authority.
Flooding concern
The worst of the remaining rainfall was expected Sunday from northern New Jersey into southern New England.
While the storm was gradually weakening, tidal flooding would stay through high-tide cycles Sunday night, said Bob Oravec, a lead forecaster with the National Weather Service in College Park, Md.

items: Some TV meteorologists want to talk about climate change. Not everyone wants to hear it

blocks.text: In New York City, water a few inches deep filled streets in the Howard Beach neighbourhood but didn't deter residents from venturing out for coffee Sunday morning.
Carole Ann Palmer, who owns Jingles Bait and Tackle in North Beach Haven, N.J., said this was the worst flooding she's seen in 10 years.
"Yesterday, I was like, oh my God, it just keeps getting higher and higher," said Palmer, who lives above the store.
The front step was swept away in the storm and she saw neighbours kayaking through the streets on Saturday.

items: Hawaii readies for arrival of Hurricane Nolo amid risks of catastrophic flooding

blocks.text: Her biggest problem on Sunday was taking her two puppies outside to relieve themselves. She had to put on waders and carry them to dry land.
"I take one at the time, carry them across the street so they can do their business and then come back, dry them off and then do the other one. It's a workout," Palmer said.
N.J. community better prepared after Sandy
Bernard Dowd waded through tidal water Sunday to get to his Sea Bright home, a day after he got back from work to find his basement "filled up like a swimming pool."

But he said the situation around his neighbourhood likely would have been much worse if it weren't for new rules requiring homeowners to raise the height of their homes in the wake of Sandy, which devastated the community.

items: The weatherman who spoke the truth – and paid the price

blocks.text: He also noticed that many around the community had lined their home and businesses with sandbags — something he wishes he would have done.
"I'm always thinking they are hyping the storm," he said.

DUBAI, UAE – Iran’s armed forces are prepared for any renewed US attacks, state media quoted army spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia saying on Sunday, after US President Donald Trump said he rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end fighting.
Akraminia said Iran’s armed forces were fully prepared for confrontation and warned that the US would suffer greater damage if it launched another attack on his country.

Separately, Iranian army commander-in-chief Amir Hatami said the war was at a critical and decisive stage, adding that Tehran would not accept a situation in which it was unable to trade while foreign powers used the region’s strategic waterways.

“If Iran cannot trade, if Iran cannot live, no one will be able to trade or live. The Strait of Hormuz is the strait of our dignity and honor, and it will not be allowed for the country’s enemies to use this major logistical chokepoint while the Iranian people are deprived.”
US President Donald Trump told Axios on Sunday, September 27, that he expected American negotiators to engage in more talks with Iran this week.
On Saturday, September 26, he had rejected the Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end fighting in the Middle East.

Iran raised the initiative at the UN General Assembly in New York, saying it had been transmitted to the Americans via Qatari mediators and that it could reopen the strategic waterway and put an end to hostilities in the region within seven days.

But in comments to reporters at the White House, Trump said: “I reject their proposal. … I rejected their deal.“They want to make a deal to open the Hormuz Strait immediately because they’re losing so badly,” he said before leaving for Tennessee.
“We’re winning tremendously.

“They want to make a deal and I think that’s fine, I like making a deal too. What they want to do is immediately open the Hormuz Strait … because they have no money coming in, because they get their money from the Hormuz Strait,” Trump said.

The US has imposed an economic blockade on Iran to put pressure on Tehran to lift its blockade of Hormuz, which has drastically reduced shipping through the strait, even though Trump again asserted that the US had control of the waterway.
The Wall Street Journal first reported that Trump had rejected the Iranian proposal, citing unnamed US officials.
It said Trump was privately sceptical that Iran would meet his demands and had told his staff that he sees a renewed bombing campaign as likely after the November US midterm elections to Congress.
A US official had said earlier that discussions with Iran through mediators were “positive and constructive.”

The Iranians also engaged their Saudi rivals regarding the Strait of Hormuz, underscoring the stakes of a seven-month-old conflict that has disrupted oil flows through a critical shipping lane and taken a toll on the global economy.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi told reporters at the United Nations on Friday, September 25, the proposed deal would trigger a seven-day countdown to reopening the strait and a pause in regional fighting.

“If there is seriousness on the US side to come to a deal and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, everything is now prepared,” Araqchi said. If the US were to agree, the warring parties could start wider talks “on mutually agreed subjects.”

That could potentially include discussions of Iran’s nuclear programme. Trump has said Tehran must never acquire a nuclear bomb, while a senior Iranian official told Reuters that Iran would show no flexibility over its nuclear program even if the US accepted its peace deal.
Iran would grant no concessions over its rights, including enriching uranium or shipping its highly enriched uranium out of the country, the official said.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show “Face the Nation,” said Tehran was ready for talks on its nuclear programme and other issues, but would not accept “bullying or coercion.”
“Iran is not seeking war, but will defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks,” Pezeshkian said, adding that it had already agreed that “we’re not supposed to develop nuclear weapons.”
Previous attempts at diplomacy have failed to end the war, which began on February 28 with US and Israeli attacks.
Since then the war has alternated between pauses and renewed strikes, killing thousands while degrading Iran’s conventional forces and damaging Iran’s already ailing economy.

Iran and its allies have retaliated by extending the conflict throughout the region. Iran has struck US allies in the Gulf with drones and missiles while its Houthi allies in Yemen have targeted Saudi interests. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Transport strike starts as fare hike takes effect
articles.summary: The transport group Samahang Manibela, Mananakay at Nagkaisang Terminal ng Transportasyon (Manibela) on Monday started its three-day transport strike as a fare hike took effect.

blocks.text: Published September 28, 2026 8:13am
The transport group Samahang Manibela, Mananakay at Nagkaisang Terminal ng Transportasyon (Manibela) on Monday started its three-day transport strike as a fare hike took effect.
Manibela conducted its transport strike in parts of Metro Manila to protest against rising fuel prices and call for higher fares.

Members of the group as well as some transport network vehicle service (TNVS) and UV Express drivers, motorcycle taxi riders and truckers, gathered at University Avenue in Quezon City early morning, according to a report of James Agustin on Unang Balita.
They proceeded in a caravan toward Philcoa and held a program to air their demands.
Among their calls are lower fuel prices, fare increase, and the removal of excise taxes and value-added tax (VAT) on petroleum products.
Some motorcycle taxi and TNVS drivers who joined the protest said they decided not to operate on Monday to support the transport strike.
Manibela chairperson Mar Valbuena said their program in Philcoa will last until around 10 a.m.
According to him, around 20,000 to 25,000 jeepney drivers in various routes in Metro Manila were expected to participate in the strike.
The group also criticized the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) over its statement that drivers who join the strike could face fines.
Fare hike
Meanwhile, the fare hike for public utility vehicles took effect Monday morning.
Based on the fare hike approved by the Department of Transportation (DOTr), P1 will be added to the current minimum fare for jeepneys, and an additional P2 for every succeeding kilometer.
The new minimum fare for traditional jeepneys is P14 (up by one peso from P13) for the first four kilometers, with an additional P2 for every succeeding kilometer (up from P1.80).
For modern jeepneys, the new minimum fare will be P17 (up from P15) for the first four kilometers, with an additional P2.40 for every succeeding kilometer (up from P2.20).
The mandatory discounts for students, senior citizens and persons with disabilities will continue to apply, the memo stated. —Joviland Rita/KG, GMA News

blocks.text: The Israeli government said on Sunday that it was revoking the diplomatic status of Dutch diplomats representing The Netherlands at the Palestinian Authority in Ramallah, the administrative capital of the Palestinian Territories.
Israeli ​Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said the move was a response to Dutch sanctions targeting illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
"Israel will not ignore measures intended to harm it," Saar wrote on social media.
He ordered Dutch diplomats operating in Ramallah to ​return their Israeli-issued diplomatic documentation within seven days.
"After this period, the diplomatic privileges and immunities granted to them by the State of Israel will expire," he added.
Israeli settlement trade ban widens across Europe
Dutch ban on settlement goods: what does it entail?
Dutch authorities announced earlier this month that they would begin enforcing a ban on settlement goods.

The ban, which applies to personal baggage as well as commercial shipments, came into force on September 22 and, in recent days, Dutch and Israeli media have reported that passengers arriving at Amsterdam's Schiphol airport from Israel had their luggage searched for banned goods.

Earlier in September, Israel also ordered the closure of ⁠the British Consulate ⁠in East Jerusalem, the United Kingdom's representative to the Palestinian Authority, after London announced similar sanctions banning the import of goods from illegal settlements.
"Any country that acts in a hostile and unilateral manner against Israel will lose influence and relevance in the region," said Saar.
France and Canada have also announced a ban on goods from settlements, but Israel has not yet taken any action against ​those two countries.
In August, Israel also banned Dutch diplomats from a Israeli-based, US-led coordination center for Gaza over what the foreign minister described as "anti-Israel measures."

articles.title: News media must stay relevant or 'society will struggle', says World News Day boss
articles.summary: World News Day aims to highlight the role of news providers in investigating and explaining important events.

blocks.text: World News Day has grown since it began in 2018, and its message that "trusted journalism matters" aims to highlight the role of news providers in investigating and explaining important events.

It comes against a backdrop of what the recent Reuters Institute report described as "anxiety, disengagement, and cynicism" towards news among the public, "but also openness to new sources and formats, and continued belief in what news at its best can offer".
Social media and video networks overtook news organisations' own websites and apps as the main source of online news last year, but are trusted less, the report said.

In another report, published earlier this month, UK media regulator Ofcom, external also said people now get news from a wider variety of sources, with YouTube "growing rapidly" and 20% of people using AI tools to access news.

But growing choice has gone hand-in-hand with greater uncertainty about who and what to believe, and traditional providers are still seen as more trustworthy, accurate and impartial than online platforms, Ofcom said.
Brkic, who founded South Africa's Daily Maverick, accepts that the media landscape has changed, and said established news organisations must respond.
"The old days are not coming back. We need to form a new equilibrium, and the only way we can do it is that if we actually join forces," he said.

"If we continue like this, we're just going to be weak individual players waiting to be taken out. If we don't change something pretty fundamentally and pretty urgently, we're just going to be roadkill."
Brkic said the mainstream media has "committed mistakes", but professional and reliable journalists play a vital role in society.
"We need to talk to our audiences and explain to them, it's not in your interest not to choose truth and trust," he said.
"We cannot function without a thing called the truth, without facts."
The definition of "the truth" is often contested, however, as seen in US President Donald Trump's long-running battle with what he labels the "fake news media".
Brkic added: "This is the information-based society. We are the infrastructure for that information-based society. And that society is actually going to really struggle without us."

articles.title: Mighty Sparrow, the Trinidad and Tobago singer known as the ‘calypso king of the world’, dies aged 91
articles.summary:
Slinger Francisco, who performed as the Mighty Sparrow, died on Sunday surrounded by family in New York

Slinger Francisco, known on stage as the Mighty Sparrow and dubbed the “calypso king…

blocks.text: Slinger Francisco, known on stage as the Mighty Sparrow and dubbed the “calypso king of the world”, has died aged 91.
Francisco, who got his breakthrough in calypso music with his 1956 hit song Jean and Dinah, died peacefully surrounded by his family in New York on Sunday, his family said in a statement.
His death came after a “brief illness,” the statement said without disclosing any other details.
“He was an institution in the entertainment industry, well admired for his skill and finesse as a singer, songwriter and mentor; beloved by many,” Francisco’s family said.

blocks.caption: Mighty Sparrow performs at the Melkweg in 1989 in Amsterdam, the Netherlands. Photograph: Frans Schellekens/Redferns

blocks.text: The Mighty Sparrow will be remembered as “a defining voice of our culture, a master storyteller and a towering figure whose music helped carry calypso from Trinidad and Tobago to the world,” the Trinbago Unified Calypsonians’ Organisation said in a statement.
Born in the coastal town of Grand Roy, Grenada, in July 1935, Francisco was just a toddler when he migrated with his parents to Trinidad and Tobago in 1937.

Trinidad and Tobago is the birthplace of calypso music, and was where the name and persona of the Mighty Sparrow emerged to produce a list of hit songs in the genre: Both of Them, Congo Man, Mr. Walker, The Lizard and many more.

Birdie, as Francisco was also affectionately known, recorded hundreds of songs in a career that spanned six decades. He performed in several countries around the world, including at famous venues such as New York City’s Madison Square Garden.
Throughout his career, Francisco’s goal was to advance the calypso art form, according to Dr Rudolph Ottley, a Trinidadian cultural historian and author.
“The Mighty Sparrow was the supreme entertainer, a cultural revolutionary and one of the world’s greatest Calypsonians,” Ottley told the Associated Press.
Trinidad and Tobago has honored the composer and performer with national awards, and in 1987 the University of the West Indies conferred an honorary doctor of letters on Francisco.

articles.title: Why some Indian civil servants become heroes for doing their jobs
articles.summary: In a system often marked by red tape and exhausting delays, officers seen to be following the rules get adulation.

blocks.text: Among the thousands of civil servants who keep India's vast government machinery running, a small number become unlikely public figures every few years.
Tukaram Mundhe, 51, is one of them.

The commissioner of Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration, he has led a series of enforcement drives since taking charge in May. His teams have inspected restaurants and other food businesses, uncovering pest infestations, poor hygiene and expired food.
He has also highlighted large gaps between what hospitals pay for common medical supplies and what patients are charged.

These actions have made Mundhe a social-media celebrity, with videos and images from inspections widely shared online. Hundreds of people have commented that they wished officers like him could be sent to fix food safety concerns in their state.
Mundhe is not alone. In Gurugram, a suburb of Delhi, district town planner RS Batth has won praise for acting against illegal construction and encroachments.
But why are these officials treated like heroes for doing their jobs?

In India, civil servants are responsible for many services people rely on every day, from issuing documents to policing, food safety and healthcare. But many are also accused of delays, bribes and making people run from pillar to post.
So when an official appears to cut through the red tape, the response can be surprisingly enthusiastic.
"What should have been normal has become exceptional," says retired civil servant Kamal Kant Jaswal.
For many citizens, delays, bureaucratic hurdles and indifferent treatment have become so familiar that efficient governance now stands out as an exception, he adds.
Mundhe is not the first official to gain recognition for doing exactly that.
One of the most prominent examples is TN Seshan, who became a household name as India's chief election commissioner in the 1990s for fearlessly enforcing rules.

Kiran Bedi, the first woman to join the officer ranks of the Indian Police Service, was nicknamed "Crane Bedi" in the early 1980s after it was widely reported that she got an illegally parked car belonging to then prime minister Indira Gandhi towed away (it was removed by a sub-inspector who reported to her, who said years later that she supported, external his decision).

Ashok Khemka became nationally known after intervening in a controversial land transaction in 2012, while police officer Neeraj Jadaun was praised for confronting a mob during deadly religious violence in Delhi in 2020.
These stories have made the idea of the "honest" or "no-nonsense" bureaucrat both familiar and rare.
Jaswal, however, points out that thousands of officials in India do their jobs without attracting public attention.
"Their work may not involve much direct contact with citizens, or may simply be less visible."
For ordinary people, however, a visit to a government office is often seen as an exhausting process.
Rajesh Singh, 43, who works at a finance company in Delhi, says he has experienced long waits to get his work done and even longer processes to solve complaints.
"What is supposed to take 24 hours, I have personally experienced being stretched to six months with no guarantee of a positive outcome even then," he says.
But an officer praised for enforcing rules can also face criticism for applying them too rigidly without taking into account ground realities.

Mundhe has been criticised by sections of the food and hospitality industry over his enforcement drives. He has rejected allegations of selective or unlawful action, saying inspections are evidence-driven and licences are suspended only in serious cases.

Batth, too, has faced flak for acting against illegal encroachments, with critics alleging his enforcement is selective and disproportionately affects vulnerable people. In several viral videos, he has said his actions are carried out strictly under town-planning rules.

Jaswal explains a street vendor's stall may be an unauthorised structure in the eyes of the law, but could be a family's only source of income. And in a country where millions migrate to cities in search of work, unsanctioned living spaces could be the only way to find a place to stay.
This tension between the law and economics helps explain why the same enforcement action can be viewed as both lawful and harsh.
Bureaucrats also face challenges of their own while carrying out their duties.

Pushpa Sundar, who briefly served as a civil servant and has written extensively on development issues, says officers can face political pressure and transfers when they refuse to comply with demands.
"They too have families, careers and financial responsibilities and it needs extraordinary courage to risk those things in order to act independently," she says.
She argues that officers need stronger institutional support when they refuse to do something illegal or improper.
Jaswal remembers facing such pressure himself.
In 1974, when he was district magistrate of Uttarkashi in what was then undivided Uttar Pradesh, a senior minister was contesting the state legislature election.
He says he had to turn down a number of demands from the minister as they were against the rules. The minister won the election and Jaswal says he got his "marching orders soon after".
But when he left for his next assignment, people stood in the summer heat for several kilometres on his way to say goodbye.
The relationship between politicians and civil servants, he says, is rarely straightforward.
Many civil servants who seek desirable postings or rely on political support choose the path of least resistance, while standing up to political pressure entails certain costs, he says.
Social media has also changed how quickly an officer can become a public sensation.
An action once limited to a district can now be filmed, shared and viewed by millions within hours.
"Social media can turn an official into a national talking point almost overnight," Sundar says.
That is partly what happened with Mundhe, whose inspection videos have turned routine enforcement into a widely watched spectacle.
Mundhe, however, sees it differently.
Speaking to the BBC last month, he said his actions were driven by public-health concerns and that businesses complying with rules had nothing to fear.
For Mundhe, the attention is beside the point. The rules already exist and his job is simply to enforce them.
But the public fascination is about more than just one officer.
When basic government functions are carried out visibly and consistently, they can seem extraordinary - particularly because so many people have come to expect otherwise.

articles.title: Failure to protect free speech could cost Labour votes at next election, says Liberty
articles.summary:
Polling for rights group shows issue is concern for voters and many feel recent policies have had negative effect

Free speech will be a big concern for voters at the next general election,…

blocks.text: Free speech will be a big concern for voters at the next general election, with the government’s current approach on the issue perceived by many to be bad for Britain, polling suggests.

Three in five people said a political party’s position on free speech would affect how they voted at a general election. The human rights organisation Liberty, which commissioned the polling from More in Common, claimed the results showed that Labour’s failure to protect free speech could cost it votes.

A significant proportion of those polled felt certain policies and rhetoric by politicians had been detrimental for free speech. For example, two in five said arrests of people for holding signs in support of the banned group Palestine Action had had a negative effect on freedom of speech. That compared with one in five who said it was positive.
Only about one in seven thought Andy Burnham cared more about protecting free speech than his predecessor, Keir Starmer.

Akiko Hart, the director of Liberty, said: “The ability to express ourselves freely makes us all who we are, and free speech is of vital importance to the British public. These findings should serve as a stark wake-up call for the government, which has lost the public’s confidence on protecting this fundamental human right.

“We’re fortunate to live in a nation shaped by many identities and perspectives, which means differences of opinion and sometimes uncomfortable views that could upset or offend others. This requires the government to adopt a consistent, non-partisan approach to safeguard everyone’s right to speak freely while protecting people from discrimination.”

The polling, released ahead of a joint Liberty and More in Common panel event at the Labour party conference on Monday, also found that more than a third of people believe politicians calling for phrases to be banned at protests is bad for free speech, compared with just over a quarter who think it is positive.

When asked about police getting greater powers to restrict protests or marches, a similar proportion – a third – believed it was good as thought it was bad. More than half of people polled said calling protests “hate marches” or “thuggery” had been bad.

Starmer called for “tougher action” against people who used phrases such as “globalise the intifada” – intifada is an Arabic word that translates as uprising or “shaking off” – at pro-Palestinian demonstrations, and there have been arrests.

The Crime and Policing Act, which received royal assent in April under Starmer, gave police increased powers to restrict protests, including requiring them to consider the “cumulative impact” of repeated demonstrations in the same area when imposing conditions. Many civil society groups were critical of the measure.

Since Palestine Action became the first direct action protest group to be proscribed, in July last year, more than 3,600 people are believed to have been arrested for showing support for the organisation, most for holding placards saying “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action”. Arrests have continued since Burnham entered office.

The UK supreme court will hear an appeal against the ban in November, having decided it is arguable that proscription represents a disproportionate interference with articles 10 and 11 of the European convention on human rights, which protect the rights of freedom of speech and protest respectively.
Both left and right have complained about so-called “cancel culture” in recent years, with each side portraying the other as the chief culprit.
Hart said: “The prime minister must show urgent leadership on an issue that is dividing the country, and change course away from heavier restrictions and towards a principled defence of free speech.”

A Home Office spokesperson said: “Freedom of speech and peaceful protest are fundamental rights that this government will always protect. But there is a clear difference between expressing a view and engaging in unlawful behaviour – such as inciting hatred and violence or supporting proscribed organisations. It is right that as a society and a government, we draw that line clearly.”
The Labour party was also approached for comment.
More in Common polled a nationally representative sample of 2,017 people in Great Britain between 11 and 15 September.

articles.title: The stories that shaped us: Rappler opens the Newsbreak Archives
articles.summary: On September 28, World News Day, annual Rappler+ members get access to the full digital archives of Newsbreak, years of fearless reporting that documented the Philippines and helped shape its history

blocks.text: On September 28, World News Day, annual Rappler+ members get access to the full digital archives of Newsbreak, years of fearless reporting that documented the Philippines and helped shape its history

items: Rappler is launching access to the full digital archives of Newsbreak, an investigative magazine founded in 2001, on World News Day.
Newsbreak has a history of exposing corruption and holding power accountable, with significant investigations into various scandals in the Philippines.
The archives aim to provide context for current events by revisiting past journalism, helping readers understand ongoing issues.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – What’s your relationship with the news? Do you simply read it, scroll past it, and move on?

Journalism does not end when the news cycle does. The investigations that uncover corruption, the stories that hold power to account, and the reporting that captures a country at a particular moment—they’re a record of how, and why, we got here.
This World News Day, Monday, September 28, Rappler is opening that record.

Annual Rappler+ members will now have access to the full digital archives of Newsbreak, the award-winning magazine born at the cusp of the EDSA II People Power revolution that ousted the Estrada regime and whose investigative tradition helped lay the foundations for Rappler.

Founded in 2001, Newsbreak started as a news weekly that scrutinized power, exposed the corrupt, explained complex events, and celebrated the good. Some of its biggest exposés include investigations into the sexual and financial misconduct of Catholic bishops; the massive cheating in the 2004 presidential elections; the comptroller mafia in the Philippine military; and the corruption in the judiciary.

The Newsbreak team eventually partnered with ABS-CBN and managed its online news platform until they helped establish Rappler in 2011. Newsbreak’s journalists include its founding editor-in-chief, Marites Dañguilan Vitug (now Rappler editor-at-large); Glenda M. Gloria (now Rappler executive editor); Chay Hofileña (now Rappler head of investigations and training); Miriam Grace Go (now Rappler managing editor); Gemma Bagayaua Mendoza (now Rappler head of strategic programs); and LeAnne Jazul (now Rappler chief photographer).

Newsbreak’s investigations from decades ago shine the light on present-day controversies. Its profiles provide perspective on public officials’ current choices. The conflicts it chronicled — and which persist to this day — enable readers to see them in a new light.
By opening the Newsbreak Archives, Rappler is reintroducing to you a brand of journalism that can help you better make sense of today’s chaos.
They’re all yours to discover now through Rappler+, whose members help sustain Rappler’s independent journalism while gaining deeper ways to engage with it.
The Newsbreak Archives aim to preserve journalism that mattered then so it can continue to inform us now.
This World News Day, read how we got here.
Access the full Newsbreak Archives with an annual Rappler+ membership.

articles.title: Hurricane Nolo still threatens Hawaii as Mexico's Baja braces for major Hurricane Polo
articles.summary:
Hurricane Nolo is moving away from Hawaiian islands but threat of heavy rain, flash floods and strong winds persists

Hurricane Nolo was moving away from the Hawaiian islands on Sunday, but…

blocks.text: Hurricane Nolo was moving away from the Hawaiian islands on Sunday, but the threat of heavy rain, flash flooding and strong winds persisted in areas of the island chain still recovering from previous storms.

Nolo was about 365 miles (585km) south-south-west of Honolulu and moving away from the Big Island at about 12mph (19kph). But the Hawaii county civil defense agency said a high wind warning, wind advisory and high surf advisory remained in effect for parts of the island through Sunday evening as Nolo’s maximum sustained winds rose to 115mph (165kph).

Nolo was expected to strengthen further and turn toward the north-west by Sunday night, though the US National Hurricane Center said the storm’s center would remain well south and south-west of the Hawaiian Islands. The storm was expected to approach the Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument, a national conservation area, early this week.

Forecasters said Nolo’s outer bands could cause life-threatening flooding and mudslides, with parts of the Big Island possibly getting up to 20in (50cm ) of rain. Heavy rain also was expected on the other islands.

“Don’t venture out if you don’t have to into the dangerous flooding environment, but also high winds. We can have trees and power lines down,” said Michael Brennan, director of the National Hurricane Center.
Heavy rain fell across the southern part of the Big Island on Saturday afternoon, prompting partial closures of one of the main highways linking Kailua-Kona in the west to Hilo in the east.

blocks.caption: Members of the Hawaii army national guard help a resident leave his home as rainwater from nearby Hurricane Nolo floods a section of Mamalahoa highway on Saturday. Photograph: Gregory Bull/AP

blocks.text: Near Naalehu, at the island’s southern point, National Guard members were seen guiding a man driving through flooded streets as he tried to leave his home during a downpour. More than 120 guard members were activated on the island, part of roughly 400 statewide after the governor issued an emergency proclamation.
Residents are still recovering from Hurricane Lala , which produced heavy rain and winds strong enough to sweep about 100 homes off their foundations on the Big Island.

About a dozen people were in the water Saturday morning at Carlsmith Beach Park in Hilo on the Big Island, despite signs saying the strand was closed. Andrea Gill was out for her regular swim before heading back home to hunker down with family.
Shop owners boarded up businesses, and events were canceled. Gill said storms are common, but hurricanes are rare. She was holding out hope that the islands might not get the full impact.
“We’re used to lots of rain. We’re not used to wind. So it’s always a blessing when we don’t get the wind from the hurricane,” Gill said.
Donald Trump recently approved an emergency declaration, authorizing the Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema) to coordinate assistance and provide funding support.
Hawaiian Electric, the state’s primary utility, said crews helping restore power in Kauai after this month’s Hurricane Lowell returned to Oahu, Maui and the Big Island in response to Nolo.

The Pacific has been unusually active this season, according to National Weather Service lead forecaster Bob Oravec, with storm activity running above average during what is already the peak of hurricane season. He said that pattern is consistent with El Niño years, when the Pacific often sees more tropical storms and hurricanes.

blocks.caption: Yellow tapes on Medano Beach on Sunday as Hurricane Polo approaches Baja California Sur, in Cabo San Lucas, Mexico. Photograph: Raquel Cunha/Reuters

blocks.text: Meanwhile, parts of Mexico’s Baja California peninsula awaited the arrival of another major hurricane with a similar name, Polo, as it edged closer after lashing other parts of the country’s southwest coast with rain and strong winds.

Hurricane Polo remained a dangerous category 3 hurricane with top sustained winds of 125mph (205kph) and was moving to the north-north-west at 12mph (19kph) about 275 miles (445km) south-south-west of Cabo San Lucas at the peninsula’s southern tip, US hurricane forecasters said Sunday afternoon. It was moving to the north at 12mph (19kph).
Mexico’s National Meteorological Service, or SMN, said in a post on the social media platform X that Polo was expected to make a Baja landfall on Monday.
Mexico’s government issued a hurricane warning along the coast of mainland Mexico from Huatabampito to Guaymas.

The Mexican navy said in a statement that it has gathered personnel and humanitarian aid in the ports of Guaymas and Mazatlan, on Mexico’s Pacific coast, and has deployed three vessels that could ship aid to coastal communities isolated by the hurricane.

One of the towns in the hurricane’s projected path is San Juanico, a small fishing community on Baja’s Pacific coast. The town has only had full-time electricity for a few years, and still experiences frequent outages. There is concern that washed-out roads could block access to the closest medical facility, about 80 minutes away in Ciudad Constitucion.
“Our people are concerned about this event,” said Gloriely Robles Meza, a manager at a small hotel. “We haven’t faced such a worrying situation in many years.”

Robles Meza said Sunday that the Mexican Army arrived in San Juanico to prepare a shelter and to provide support for possible emergencies. An electrical crew was also there to prepare for Polo’s arrival.

Also on Sunday, tropical storm Rachel formed well off Mexico’s south-west coast, the Miami-based US hurricane center said. It added that Rachel had maximum sustained winds of 40mph (65kph) and was located about 300 miles (485km ) south of Acapulco, Mexico. No coastal watches or warnings were in effect.

blocks.text: Published September 28, 2026 6:38am
The Senate impeachment court in session for the trial of Vice President Sara Duterte. Senate/File
Sara Duterte impeachment trial Day 30: What to expect

The Senate impeachment court is expected to continue on Monday, September 28, the witness cross-examinations and the presentation of evidence regarding alleged unexplained wealth and corporate ties of Vice President Sara Duterte.

It can be recalled that the impeachment court issued a fresh subpoena for Davao City Mayor Sebastian "Baste" Duterte, Atty. Gary Samonte, and Police Major Jerickson Sangalang for September 28 to 30, Monday to Wednesday.

The subpoena ad testificandum et duces tecum for the Davao City top official was issued by the Senate impeachment court as GenCorp Industries Inc., which the vice president declared as one of her business interests in her 2024 and 2025 Statements of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALNs), secured contracts with the Davao City government worth about P30 million.
The subpoena was already received by Baste's office.
But the Davao City mayor already denied that he was aware of his sister's alleged link to GenCorp Industries Inc.

During Day 28 of the impeachment trial on Tuesday, the House prosecution presented Philippine Government Electronic Procurement System (PhilGEPS) Division Chief Rendell Sopeña, who testified that the Philippine Health Insurance Corp. (PhilHealth) Region 11 alone awarded 33 contracts to GenCorp.

The House prosecution said they were presenting Sopeña and GenCorp.-won contracts as evidence to prove the subsection of Article 2 of the Articles of Impeachment on unexplained wealth, which is the Vice President’s non-divestment of other business and financial interests.
Sopeña committed to return on Monday as the impeachment will continue tackling the alleged unexplained wealth of the vice president. —Vince Angelo Ferreras/KG, GMA News

articles.title: Inside Yemen's front-line city as Houthis battle for control
articles.summary: In rare access to Yemen's conflict zone the BBC travels to the front line with pro-government soldiers.

blocks.text: Watch: Correspondent takes cover as approaching drone interrupts report
ByNawal Al-Maghafi
Senior international investigations correspondentReporting fromTaiz, Yemen
"This is the first drone," said the soldier accompanying us in south-western Yemen. "It's usually followed by an attack."
The buzzing sound overhead got louder as we took cover under the bushes, before climbing back into the vehicle and driving away.
Within about 10 minutes, the loud thuds of strikes followed, one after another, though it was unclear where they landed.
It is hard to tell where the front line begins in the mountains south-west of the city of Taiz.

Saudi-backed pro-government forces are battling to push back Houthi fighters, who swept down the coast of the Red Sea earlier this month, taking control of a key shipping chokepoint and escalating Yemen's civil war.
We travelled with government forces from Taiz through checkpoints to the line where their control ends and no man's land begins, in order to see the fighting up close.

blocks.caption: Two-panel map of Yemen showing Houthi-controlled territory and contested areas on 24 September. Houthi-controlled territory, shaded pink, covers much of western Yemen including Sanaa and extends south along the Red Sea coast towards the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Purple-striped areas mark contested te…

blocks.text: Homes are scattered across the slopes, but many stand abandoned after families fled to escape the fighting.
It is eerily quiet, no sound of the cars or motorbikes that are continuously whizzing through the city. All you can hear is the bleating of livestock and the sound of incoming and outgoing fire.
"Two mortars landed here on my property," said Ali, sitting outside his home with a herd of goats, about 1km (0.6 miles) from the front line.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Ali has remained at home under mortar fire to look after his goats

blocks.text: Image source, Liam Weir/BBC
Ali has remained at home under mortar fire to look after his goats
He told me he had sent his children to a displacement camp because they could no longer cope with the shelling and gunfire. He had stayed with his wife and sisters to look after their animals.
"I am terrified," he said, "but I have no choice, we will all go hungry without our animals and die anyway."

He gave only his first name, fearful of repercussions if the Houthis take over the area in the days ahead. Contacts from the Houthi side have told us they are consolidating troops, preparing for a major offensive. When we asked government forces about this they said they are aware and were preparing too.

At the closest checkpoint to the front line, we met some fighters who had just returned from positions high on the mountain, just a few hundred metres from advancing Houthis. One of them said the bodies of 18 government soldiers lay in an area his unit could fire across but not reach.
"We shoot over them, but we can't pull them out," he said.

Fighting around Taiz has intensified since the Houthis seized the strategic Red Sea port of Mokha, 85km to the west of the city, on 10 September, after a ceasefire that had largely held for four years unravelled.

The group took control of a swathe of territory overlooking the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait – a crucial shipping corridor linking Europe and Asia. This contributed to a rise in oil prices as fears rose of further disruption to supplies from the region.

blocks.caption: Detailed map of Taiz in south-western Yemen showing areas of territorial control on 20 September. Houthi-controlled territory is shaded pink and surrounds much of the city, while white areas mark territory outside Houthi control and purple diagonal stripes indicate contested areas.

blocks.text: Taiz is Yemen's third biggest city and its cultural capital, and is home to close to a million people. It sits at a vital intersection between Houthi-controlled areas in northern Yemen and government-held ones in the south – and is hemmed in by front lines in several directions.

Government forces hold the centre of Taiz, while Houthi positions lie to its north and east. The fiercest recent fighting has been on the western approaches, where the two sides are contesting high ground overlooking the city's route south. If the Houthis secure these areas, government forces could find it much harder to retake Mokha.
We travelled to Taiz from Aden in the south, where Yemen's internationally recognised Presidential Leadership Council and government are based.
About 30 checkpoints along the route marked stretches of road controlled by different commanders – a clear sign of the fractured make-up of the forces fighting on the government side.

As we neared the city, ambulances began to pass us. We counted at least five within half an hour, heading towards Taiz's main hospital. It was clear that we were driving into a city at the heart of a brutal battle.

We arrived after dark. The shops were lit, the restaurants were packed and children were playing in the streets. But every so often, other sounds broke through – the thud of shelling and the crack of gunfire from the mountains around the city.

blocks.caption: Image caption, An international coalition led by Saudi Arabia is providing the Yemeni government with weapons

blocks.text: An international coalition led by Saudi Arabia is providing the Yemeni government with weapons

Taiz has been a major battleground in the country's devastating civil war. After ousting the government from Sanaa in 2015, the Houthis attempted to also seize control of Taiz but were driven out of most of the city by local militiamen.
Now, in their latest offensive, Houthis are making extensive use of drones alongside other weapons.

Their main outside supplier is Iran, which has provided weapons, funding and military advice, according to Saudi Arabia, Western countries and UN experts. Iran, however, has previously denied supplying weapons to the Houthis and says it only supports them politically.
There have been persistent reports over many years of the Houthis recruiting child soldiers, and a government soldier told us he had faced them on the front line.
"It's difficult to look at a Yemeni child and shoot at him. But then they are pointing the gun at you and you have to defend yourself," he said.
The Houthis signed an "action plan" with the UN in 2022 pledging to end the practice. The BBC has also spoken to teenagers serving with government forces.

Meanwhile a coalition led by Saudi Arabia is backing the Yemeni government, and providing it with weapons. The Saudi military has carried out hundreds of air strikes on Houthi positions on the Red Sea coast, while the Houthis have launched drones and missiles at cities and infrastructure in south-western Saudi Arabia.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Twelve-year-old Ghana was seriously injured by a mortar while herding goats

blocks.text: Image source, Liam Weir/BBC News
Twelve-year-old Ghana was seriously injured by a mortar while herding goats
In the evening, at al-Thawra hospital in Taiz, casualties from the front lines were being brought into an intensive care unit where every bed we saw was occupied.
Some patients were fighters, others were civilians. Twelve-year-old Ghana Nabeel had been herding goats when shrapnel struck her head. Her family said an incoming Houthi mortar had landed nearby.
She lay unconscious, her head wrapped in bandages, her face swollen and bruised. Her family were waiting at her bedside to learn what life might be like if she wakes up.
A doctor told me the injury had damaged her brain. "She will never be the same again," he said.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The UN says 130,000 people have been displaced by fighting in Yemen so far this month

blocks.text: The UN says 130,000 people have been displaced by fighting in Yemen so far this month
About 20km south of Taiz, at the al-Monig displacement camp, families who had fled Mokha and villages hit by fighting were arriving, among hundreds of tents.
We were told that 200 families had arrived in the previous 10 days.
Maryam Saleh, not her real name, had come a week earlier from Mokha with her husband and five children. The youngest is aged seven. Maryam sat weaving a hat to sell so she could buy food for the day.
"We walked barefoot and we didn't carry anything with us, just our children," she told me.

Her nephew was killed by shrapnel from a mortar as they fled, she said. He had been walking behind her. She described clashes and sniping both ahead of and behind the family and said she then saw armed men on the mountain.
"We thought we were finished," she said. The children were screaming and crying, but the family kept walking, she added.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Fatma Mohammed Saleh, who cannot walk, says she crawled for two days before being given a lift by a motorcyclist

blocks.text: Fatma Mohammed Saleh, who cannot walk, says she crawled for two days before being given a lift by a motorcyclist

Fatma Mohammed Saleh was lying on an empty rice sack outside another family's tent. She has a disability and cannot walk, and told me she had nowhere of her own to sleep: "I have nothing… no shelter, no mattress, no family. Nothing."
Fatma said she had been with her two sons and their children when the fighting reached their village. But she was slowing them down so told them to take the children and run, she said.
She spent the next two days crawling on her hands and knees, she said.
"I was crawling and the bullets are coming from here and the shells are there. And the bullets are here, and the shells are here. And above me it was like thunder. I was praying to God."
A man on a motorbike then saw her and drove her to the camp, she said. She has not seen her family since.
On 22 September, the UN refugee agency said more than 130,000 people had been displaced across Yemen so far this month, on top of 5.2 million already displaced by the civil war.
It warned that another 100,000 could – like Fatma – be forced from their homes over the next three months.
Additional reporting by Jasmin Dyer

articles.title: Pilot identified in fatal helicopter crash outside of Montreal
articles.summary: The pilot of a fatal helicopter crash in Sainte-Brigide-d'Iberville, outside of Montreal on Saturday has been identified as Suzanne Jutras.

image.caption: A police cruiser is parked just off the Rang des Écossais in Sainte-Brigide-D'Iberville after a helicopter crashed in a field killing all four occupants. (Alexandre Silberman/CBC)

blocks.text: Montreal·New
The pilot of a fatal helicopter crash in Sainte-Brigide-d'Iberville, outside of Montreal on Saturday has been identified as Suzanne Jutras.
Suzanne Jutras was 'our favourite pilot,' say Quebec festival organizers
The pilot involved in a fatal helicopter crash in Sainte-Brigide-d'Iberville, Que., outside of Montreal on Saturday has been identified.
The plane crashed in a corn field near near Rang des Écossais, just off Highway 10, around 2:30 p.m., killing all four occupants — including pilot Suzanne Jutras.

Initially, the Sûreté du Québec said they believed the aircraft had experienced difficulties shortly after takeoff leading to the crash. In an update Sunday, however, SQ spokesperson Valérie Beauchamp said the crash happened when the aircraft was returning.
Jutras, a commercial pilot, was based in Sainte-Brigide-d'Iberville, according to a Linkedin profile in her name.
She regularly offered helicopter tours, including last weekend at les Félixeries, a cultural and community festival in Saint-Félix-de-Kingsey, near Drummondville.
Festival organizers confirmed to CBC News that Jutras was the pilot killed in Saturday's crash.

items: Helicopter crashes outside Montreal, killing all 4 occupants

blocks.text: In a post on social media, les Félixeries paid tribute to Jutras, calling her their "favourite pilot of the past three years."
"We extend our deepest sympathies to her partner, family, friends, and everyone who had the privilege of knowing her through her passion," the French-language post said.
Jutras had plenty of experience, said one of her friends, a fellow pilot who spoke to Radio-Canada off camera.
Radio host was on board
The SQ did not confirm the identities of the victims, referring any inquiries to the Quebec coroner's office.
The office did not respond in time for publication.
CBC has learned, however, that one of the occupants was Gabriel Jasmin, a radio host and advertising producer at Énergie Sherbrooke radio.
Énergie 106.1 took to social media to express their condolences to Jasmin's loved ones, including his wife and daughter and his team at Bell Media.
"Our thoughts are with all those affected by his passing," the post reads.
A social media post written by his widow says the other two passengers on board the helicopter were relatives.
The SQ says it had concluded its investigation and the matter is now in the hands of the Transportation Safety Board of Canada.
Federal Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon said on Saturday that he would appoint a minister's observer to monitor the response alongside the TSB.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Annabelle Olivier is a digital journalist at CBC Montreal. She previously worked at Global News as an online producer. You can reach her at anne.isabelle.olivier@cbc.ca.
With files from Radio-Canada

articles.title: Blanche defends Trump’s White House media ban: ‘It’s a privilege … not a right’
articles.summary:
US attorney general argues that president is ‘sick and tired’ of inaccurate reporting by CNN, MS Now and Politico

Donald Trump’s…

blocks.text: Donald Trump’s attorney general Todd Blanche argued on Sunday that the administration banned three news outlets from the White House because it is “privilege … not a right” to be there.

Appearing on the ABC News program This Week during the second week of the White House’s dispute over press credentialing and access, Blanche also said that the administration took the decision to ban CNN, MS Now and Politico beginning on 19 September because the president was “sick and tired” of what he considered to be those media outlets’ inaccurate reporting.

On Thursday, a judge issued a temporary restraining order requiring the White House to temporarily restore the credentials of affected journalists, and they were allowed entry to the executive complex.
But on Saturday, CNN said its journalists were barred from joining the press pool traveling with the president on Air Force One.

“The president hasn’t denied access,” Blanche told the outlet. “That’s not the right way to describe it.” He pointed to Trump’s comments that he is “sick and tired” of certain media outlets’ reporting that the president considers inaccurate.
“There’s still obviously litigation going on, but the important thing … is to know that … being in the White House is a privilege. It’s not a right,” Blanche said.

The continuing dispute between the administration and the White House press corp had appeared to be resolving before CNN was again blocked for pool coverage. That was after outlets stood in solidarity with CNN, MS Now and Politico by briefly refusing to carry pool TV feeds of the president.
On ABC, Blanche said it wasn’t unusual for a news outlet to not be allowed on to the president’s plane.
“The White House routinely decides who can go on Air Force One,” Blanche said. “This wasn’t a one-time denial of CNN. There’s all kinds of times when certain reporters are not flying or are flying.
“It’s not unusual, and as a matter of fact, it’s common every time the president travels that he and his team decide which reporters get to travel with the president.”
Blanche repeated the administration’s position that the affected three outlets’ reporting amounted to a “national security problem”.

Trump has said that there was not any “particular reason” for the action against CNN, MS Now and Politico, arguing “they purposely write negative news, and they do that because they want to … diminished the Republicans and a Republican administration”.

In the ruling to temporarily restore the three banned outlets’ White House access for 14 days, US district judge Timothy Kelly said there was nothing in the record suggesting that revocation of the press passes was motivated by national security concerns.

“Certainly, that is not what President Trump said when he announced that he was ‘banning’ plaintiffs from the White House – instead, he focused on the alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity of plaintiffs’ reporting,” Kelly wrote in his ruling.

Trump was faced with a gloomy political landscape with just over a month before the federal midterm elections in November. A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found Trump’s overall public approval rating to be at 32%, an all-time low.

But confidence in the news media polls lower, with just 28% expressing a “great deal” or “fair amount” of trust in newspapers, television channels and radio outlets to report the news fully, accurately and fairly, according to a 2025 Gallup survey.

Bill Clinton recently commented on the battle between what the news media see as a crude effort at censorship and a denial of constitutional rights – and what the White House views as unfairly negative reporting.

“There were lots of times when I wanted to ban the White House press corps,” the former president said at the Clinton Global Initiative 2026 summit. “And there’s a reason we have a constitution – because none of us are immune from being pissed off.
“But I’m glad I never did, and I’m glad I couldn’t. And these people shouldn’t. The law should be what it is.”
Blanche was asked what the US constitution’s first amendment – which guarantees the right to a free press – meant to him.

“The law says – what the free press can do is they are free to report whatever they want,” Blanche remarked. “Of course, they can. But when it comes to the White House, it is the people’s house. It is a privilege and not a right to be there.”
He added that “it is absolutely the president’s duty to make sure that the American people are hearing accurate news.”
